text: Here's a real problem the last two lessons' tools can't solve on their own: how do you write one function that works correctly for many different types, without just giving up and typing everything any? Generics are the answer.

Take a function that returns the first element of any array. Typing the array any slash any works — it compiles for every array you throw at it. But look at what you get back: also any, every single time. Pass in numbers, you get any. Pass in strings, you get any. The specific type information you actually wanted preserved is just gone.

A generic fixes this with one small change. T here is a placeholder — not a real type, a stand-in for whatever type gets used at each specific call site. Call first with an array of numbers, and T becomes number for that call; the return type follows along automatically. Call it with strings instead, and T becomes string that time. And notice: no manual annotation at the call site at all — TypeScript infers T from the argument you actually passed in.

Reading the syntax left to right: angle brackets T declares that this function has a placeholder type available to use. arr colon T array means the parameter is an array of whatever T turns out to be. And the final colon T, on the return type, says the output matches that exact same placeholder — guaranteeing the relationship between input and output type, whatever T ends up being.

A generic function isn't limited to one placeholder. Here, pair takes two independent ones, K and V, used for a key and a value respectively. TypeScript infers each independently from its own argument — pass a string and a number, and the result comes back typed as exactly a string-number pair, no annotation required anywhere.

This is exactly the trick real blockchain libraries lean on constantly. One function, callContract, handles calling any method on any contract by name. But because its return type is generic, specifying the type when you call it — bigint here, for a balance — still gives you back a correctly typed result for that specific call, instead of settling for any.

That's generics, at the basics: one function, staying type-safe for whatever type actually shows up at each call site. Next lesson closes this chapter with the flip side of all of this — narrowing a broader type down to something specific, at runtime, based on an actual check.
